banff-national-park.story: Welcome, traveller, to Banff National Park, Canada’s first national park, established in 1885 as Rocky Mountains Park. It lies in Alberta’s Rocky Mountains and encompasses 6,641 square kilometres of mountainous terrain, with many glaciers and ice fields, dense coniferous forest, and alpine landscapes. Its glaciers are now found only on the mountain slopes, including the Columbia Icefield, the largest uninterrupted glacial mass in the Rockies, and erosion from water and ice has carved the mountains into their current shapes. There, mammal species such as the grizzly bear, cougar, wolverine, elk, bighorn sheep and moose are found, along with hundreds of bird species.
banff-national-park.name: Banff National Park

castle-mountain.story: Halfway between Banff and Lake Louise in Banff National Park, Castle Mountain—Miistukskoowa—stands as the easternmost mountain of the Main Ranges in the Bow Valley, its castle-like appearance shaped by erosion acting at different rates on alternating softer shale and harder limestone, dolomite, and quartzite. The Castle Mountain Fault thrust older sedimentary and metamorphic rocks over the younger rocks at its base, and in 1858 James Hector named the mountain for its castle-like look; from 1946 to 1979 it was known as Mount Eisenhower, and after the original name was restored, a southeastern pinnacle became Eisenhower Tower. Though it looks nearly inaccessible from the Trans-Canada Highway, you can ascend from the backside on the northeastern slopes, and the trail to Rockbound Lake leads hikers around the eastern side. Nearby are the remains of Silver City and the Castle Mountain Internment Camp, while the massif contains Helena Ridge, Stuart Knob, and Television Peak, the latter named for the TV repeater on top.
castle-mountain.name: Castle Mountain

kicking-horse-pass.story: Traveller, you are in Kicking Horse Pass, a high mountain pass across the Continental Divide of the Americas in the Canadian Rockies, on the Alberta–British Columbia border within Yoho and Banff national parks. First Nations had known and used this pass, and it was first explored by Europeans in 1858 by the Palliser Expedition led by Captain John Palliser. The pass and the adjacent Kicking Horse River were named after James Hector, who was kicked by his horse while attempting to rescue another horse that had gone into the river, and Hector was led to the pass by his Stoney Nakoda guide Hector Nimrod. Here, Divide Creek forks onto both sides of the continental divide, and Hector’s summary tells of a large stream, a sharp turn, and a fall about 40 feet high where perpendicular rocks contract the channel.
kicking-horse-pass.name: Kicking Horse Pass

mount-temple-alberta.story: As you make your way through Banff National Park in the Canadian Rockies of Alberta, Mount Temple stands in the Bow River Valley between Paradise Creek and Moraine Creek. It is the highest peak in the Lake Louise area and dominates the western landscape along the Trans-Canada Highway from Castle Junction to Lake Louise. In 1884, George Mercer Dawson named the mountain after Sir Richard Temple, who visited the Canadian Rockies that same year. Mount Temple was the first 11,000-foot peak to be climbed in the Canadian segment of the Rocky Mountains.
mount-temple-alberta.name: Mount Temple (Alberta)

saddle-mountain-alberta.story: For a traveller, Saddle Mountain is a 2,433-metre summit in Alberta, Canada, located in the Bow Valley within Banff National Park and part of the Bow Range of the Canadian Rockies. Lake Louise townsite is situated 4 kilometres to the northeast, the Continental Divide is 6 kilometres to the west, and the nearest higher neighbor is Fairview Mountain, 1.2 km to the northwest. The peak is visible from Alberta Highway 1 to the east and is prominent in the iconic photographs taken from Morant's Curve; the Paradise Valley Trail leads from Lake Louise to Saddleback Pass, and from the pass an off-trail scramble leads to the top, where the summit offers one of the finest views of the area, including the Bow Valley and a close view of the impressive north face of Mount Temple. Precipitation runoff from Saddle Mountain drains into tributaries of the Bow River, and topographic relief is modest as the summit rises over 600 meters above Paradise Creek in one kilometer and nearly 900 meters above the Bow River in 3 km.
saddle-mountain-alberta.name: Saddle Mountain (Alberta)

neptuak-mountain.story: Traveller, Neptuak Mountain was named by Samuel E.S. Allen in 1894, and “Neptuak” is the Stoney Indian word for “nine” because it is peak #9 in the Valley of the Ten Peaks. It sits on the Continental Divide, also the British Columbia-Alberta border in this region, in the Bow Range of the Park Ranges of the Canadian Rockies, and its summit is a tripoint for Banff National Park, Kootenay National Park, and Yoho National Park, where the three parks share a common border. The first ascent was made on September 2, 1902 by J. Norman Collie, Hugh E.M. Stutfield, G.M. Weed, H. Woolley, guided by Christian Kaufmann, while on April 10, 2016 Luka Lindič and Marc-André Leclerc completed the first ascent via the NE face and named the route “Psychological Effect (700m, WI5+ M7).” Brette Harrington and Tony McLane made the second ascent via the NE face on August 5, 2020, and like other mountains in Banff Park, Neptuak is composed of sedimentary rock laid down during the Precambrian to Jurassic periods, formed in shallow seas and pushed east over younger rock during the Laramide orogeny.
neptuak-mountain.name: Neptuak Mountain

mount-fay.story: For a traveller in the Canadian Rockies, Mount Fay is a mountain on the Continental Divide and part of the backdrop to Moraine Lake in the Valley of the Ten Peaks of Banff National Park. It was named in 1902 for Charles E. Fay, an early explorer of the Canadian Rockies who was a member of the party who attempted Mount Lefroy in 1896 when the first mountaineer to be killed in the Canadian Rockies occurred. In 1904, Gertrude Benham made the first ascent ahead of the mountain's namesake alpinist Charles E. Fay, and on December 22, 1937, E.R. Gibson, Doug Crosby, and Bob Hind made the first winter ascent. Like other mountains in Banff Park, Mount Fay is composed of sedimentary rock laid down during the Precambrian to Jurassic periods, formed in shallow seas and pushed east over the top of younger rock during the Laramide orogeny.
mount-fay.name: Mount Fay

narao-peak.story: Traveller, as you travel Highway 1 through British Columbia, Canada, Narao Peak is visible just south-southwest of Kicking Horse Pass, within Yoho National Park. This 2,974-metre summit in the Bow Range of the Canadian Rockies rises 1,240 metres above the Narao Lakes in 2 km, and if you are en route to Lake O'Hara you pass below its western base. Its name comes from the Stoney word meaning “hit in the stomach,” perhaps related to an 1858 Palliser expedition incident when a spooked horse kicked James Hector unconscious near here. The peak’s toponym was officially adopted on April 3, 1952, after a first ascent in 1913 and a name given by cartographer Samuel E.S. Allen.
narao-peak.name: Narao Peak
